 ‘You Can See Everything’: Nathan Fielder, Lance Oppenheim Deemed Ineligible for DGA’s Top Prize
 The three-hour Elizabeth Holmes project will only be eligible in the guild’s documentary category
 Casey Loving 
 October 27, 2026 @ 12:09 PM 
 Share on Social Media
 Share on Facebook 
 Share on X (formerly Twitter) 
 Share on LinkedIn 
 Share on Email 
 Nathan Fielder in "You Can See Everything" (Credit: A24) 
 Getting your Trinity Audio player ready… 
 Warning: This article contains spoilers for “You Can See Everything.” 
 “ You Can See Everything ” is facing one of its first hurdles in what is sure to be a unique awards season for the Nathan Fielder/Lance Oppenheim documentary.
 Read Next 
 How 'You Can See Everything' Could Crack $100 Million at the Box Office | Analysis 
 The film, which follows Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes in the days leading up to and following her imprisonment for defrauding investors, will not be allowed to compete for the top prize at the Directors Guild of America Awards, TheWrap has learned. This means the film will only be eligible for the Outstanding Directorial Achievement in Documentary prize.
 This determination is consistent with DGA rules, which state that “re-releases, animated films and documentaries are not eligible” for Outstanding Directorial Achievement in Theatrical Feature Film. This is not consistent with the Academy Awards, which have no such criteria for Best Picture.
 “You Can See Everything” is an odd case for this awards season. While the film is undeniably a documentary, its DNA is imbued with enough fictional elements (deriving from Fielder’s history as a TV prankster) that throw it off the course of a traditional doc. Aspects such as (spoiler alert!) Amanda Seyfried’s presence and performance as Holmes muddy the documentary waters.
 This puts “You Can See Everything” in a very odd and potentially history-making position. The film doesn’t feel like the kind of feature that the Academy’s documentary branch would traditionally go for, yet its box office performance and incredibly positive reception have it poised to possibly become the first doc in history nominated for Best Picture. Seyfried also seems like a strong contender for Best Supporting Actress, which would make her the first performer ever nominated for a documentary.
